An O(1) average membership test replaces an O(n) search, cutting the total to O(n^3). Because the array is sorted, (nums[a], nums[b], need, nums[d]) is already ordered, and the tuple set handles duplicates. Costs: O(n) extra space per (a, b) round, and set discipline (clear it for each new pair).
approaches.algorithm:
1. Sort nums; prepare the result set 'found'.
2. For each a, for each b > a: create a FRESH empty set 'seen'.
3. For d from b+1 upward: compute need = target - nums[a] - nums[b] - nums[d].
4. If need is in 'seen', record the quadruplet (nums[a], nums[b], need, nums[d]).
5. Add nums[d] to 'seen' so it can serve as a third number for later d's.
6. Return the found set as a sorted list of lists.
approaches.code:
def four_sum(nums: List[int], target: int) -> List[List[int]]:
    # Fix three numbers, find the missing one with a hash set of seen values.
    nums = sorted(nums)                   # sorted input keeps quadruplets ordered
    n = len(nums)                         # total numbers
    found = set()                         # tuple set removes duplicate quadruplets
    for a in range(n):                    # first fixed number
        for b in range(a + 1, n):         # second fixed number
            seen = set()                  # values seen strictly between b and d
            for d in range(b + 1, n):     # scan candidates for the FOURTH number
                need = target - nums[a] - nums[b] - nums[d]   # required third value
                if need in seen:          # a valid third number sits between b and d
                    quad = (nums[a], nums[b], need, nums[d])  # already in sorted order
                    found.add(quad)       # set membership kills duplicates
                seen.add(nums[d])         # nums[d] may serve as a THIRD number later
    return [list(q) for q in sorted(found)]   # deterministic sorted output

complexity.time: O(n^3) — two fixed loops plus a linear scan with O(1) lookups
complexity.space: O(n) — the per-pair 'seen' set (plus the answer set)

approaches.name: Optimal
approaches.intuition: Sort once, fix the first two numbers with loops i and j, and hunt the remaining pair with TWO POINTERS instead of a hash set: left starts just after j, right at the array's end. If their sum undershoots need, only moving left rightward can help; if it overshoots, only moving right leftward can — so each (i, j) round costs one linear sweep and O(1) extra space. Duplicates are prevented at the source: skip i when nums[i] equals its predecessor, skip j the same way (within its level), and after recording a hit, slide both pointers past all equal values. Same O(n^3) time as hashing but with no per-round set, no tuple hashing, and the output emerges pre-sorted — this is the version interviewers expect.
approaches.algorithm:
1. Sort nums; let n = len(nums), result = [].
2. Loop i from 0 to n-4; if i > 0 and nums[i] == nums[i-1], continue (duplicate first number).
3. Loop j from i+1 to n-3; if j > i+1 and nums[j] == nums[j-1], continue (duplicate second number).
4. Set need = target - nums[i] - nums[j]; set left = j+1, right = n-1.
5. While left < right: compute pair = nums[left] + nums[right]. If pair == need, record [nums[i], nums[j], nums[left], nums[right]], move both pointers inward, then keep sliding each past duplicates of the value it just used.
6. Else if pair < need, advance left; else retreat right.
7. After both loops finish, return result.
approaches.code:
def four_sum(nums: List[int], target: int) -> List[List[int]]:
    # Sort, fix the first two numbers, close the last two with two pointers.
    nums = sorted(nums)                   # sorted order powers pointers + dedupe
    n = len(nums)                         # total numbers available
    result = []                           # unique quadruplets, collected in order
    for i in range(n - 3):                # first number needs 3 slots after it
        if i > 0 and nums[i] == nums[i - 1]:
            continue                      # same first value as before -> only dupes
        for j in range(i + 1, n - 2):     # second number needs 2 slots after it
            if j > i + 1 and nums[j] == nums[j - 1]:
                continue                  # same second value as before -> only dupes
            need = target - nums[i] - nums[j]   # what the last two must sum to
            left, right = j + 1, n - 1    # pointers closing in from both ends
            while left < right:           # scan the remaining window
                pair = nums[left] + nums[right]   # current candidate pair sum
                if pair == need:          # hit: a full quadruplet reaches target
                    result.append([nums[i], nums[j], nums[left], nums[right]])
                    left += 1             # step past the third number just used
                    right -= 1            # and past the matching fourth number
                    while left < right and nums[left] == nums[left - 1]:
                        left += 1         # skip duplicate third values
                    while left < right and nums[right] == nums[right + 1]:
                        right -= 1        # skip duplicate fourth values
                elif pair < need:         # undershoot -> need a bigger left value
                    left += 1             # move the left pointer outward
                else:                     # overshoot -> need a smaller right value
                    right -= 1            # pull the right pointer inward
    return result                         # every unique quadruplet, sorted inside

complexity.time: O(n^3) — O(n^2) fixed pairs, each with an O(n) two-pointer sweep
complexity.space: O(1) — pointers only, ignoring the output list (O(n log n) sort may use O(n))

Four Sum.tests:
res = four_sum([1, 0, -1, 0, -2, 2], 0)
assert sorted(map(tuple, res)) == [(-2, -1, 1, 2), (-2, 0, 0, 2), (-1, 0, 0, 1)]
res2 = four_sum([2, 2, 2, 2, 2], 8)
assert sorted(map(tuple, res2)) == [(2, 2, 2, 2)]        # heavy-duplicate stress test
assert four_sum([1, 2, 3], 6) == []                      # edge: fewer than 4 numbers
res3 = four_sum([-3, -1, 0, 2, 4, 5], 0)
assert sorted(map(tuple, res3)) == [(-3, -1, 0, 4)]
res4 = four_sum([0, 0, 0, 0], 0)
assert sorted(map(tuple, res4)) == [(0, 0, 0, 0)]        # exactly four equal elements

Largest Subarray with 0 Sum.title: Largest Subarray with 0 Sum
Largest Subarray with 0 Sum.problemStatement: You are given an array arr of integers — positives, negatives, and zeros mixed freely. Find the LENGTH of the longest contiguous subarray whose elements sum to exactly 0, and return that length (return 0 if no such subarray exists at all). You return only the length, not the subarray itself. Example: in [15, -2, 2, -8, 1, 7, 10, 23], the slice [-2, 2, -8, 1, 7] sums to 0 and has length 5 — nothing longer works. The brute-force answer checks all O(n^2) subarrays, but the key insight is about prefix sums: if the running total from the start is EQUAL at two positions, everything between those positions must cancel to zero, which turns the whole problem into a single hash-map pass.

examples.explanation: Watch the running prefix sums: 15, 13, 15, 7, 8, 15, 25, 48. The value 15 appears after index 0, after index 2, and after index 5. Equal prefix sums mean the elements between them cancel out: from just after index 0 to index 5 — the slice [-2, 2, -8, 1, 7] — the sum is 15 - 15 = 0, and its length is 5 - 0 = 5. The shorter repeat (indices 1..2, [-2, 2]) gives length 2. The longest gap between equal prefix sums is 5, so the answer is 5.
All elements are positive, so every subarray sums to something greater than 0 — no zero-sum subarray exists and the answer is 0.
Both [1, 0, -1] (indices 0..2) and [0, -1, 1] (indices 1..3) sum to 0 with length 3; nothing of length 4 works since the total sum is 1.

edgeCases: No zero-sum subarray at all (e.g. all positives): the function must return 0, which falls out naturally only if 'best' starts at 0.
A zero-sum prefix that starts at index 0 (e.g. [1, -1, 5]): handled ONLY by seeding the map with {0: -1} — forget it and you silently miss every prefix window.
The same prefix sum appearing three or more times: you must keep the EARLIEST index and never overwrite it, otherwise later windows get measured too short.
An array of all zeros ([0, 0, 0]): the whole array is the answer (length 3), stressing that a repeated prefix sum of 0 keeps stretching from the seeded index -1.
A single 0 element ([5, 0, 7]): answer is 1 — the map approach finds it because prefix repeats across the lone zero.
followUps: Return the actual subarray (start and end indices), not just the length — what extra bookkeeping do you need at the moment 'best' improves?
Count ALL zero-sum subarrays instead of the longest: with f occurrences of one prefix value you get C(f, 2) windows — how does the map change?
Longest subarray summing to K (not 0): show that looking up prefix - K in the same first-occurrence map solves it, and where {0: -1} goes.
The array arrives as a stream too large for memory: can you still answer 'longest zero-sum window so far' online, and what is the memory cost of the prefix map?
prerequisites: Prefix sums: sum(arr[l..r]) = prefix[r] - prefix[l-1], so equal prefixes at two spots mean the slice between them sums to 0.
The first-occurrence hash-map trick: store only the EARLIEST index of each prefix value to maximize later window lengths.
The virtual empty prefix: seeding {0: -1} represents the sum of zero elements 'before' index 0, catching windows that start at the very beginning.
Python dict lookups and inserts are O(1) on average — the whole pass stays linear.
The running-max pattern: best = max(best, candidate) inside a single loop.

approaches.name: Brute Force
approaches.intuition: Check every contiguous subarray. The one clever economy: for a fixed start index, do not re-sum each candidate subarray from scratch — keep a running total and extend it one element at a time, so each (start, end) pair costs O(1) after the previous one. Whenever the running total hits exactly 0, the window start..end is a zero-sum subarray; record its length if it beats the best so far. Still, there are O(n^2) windows, and with n = 10^5 that is ~5 billion elementary steps — the recomputation across DIFFERENT start indices is the waste the prefix-sum insight eliminates.
approaches.algorithm:
1. Let n = len(arr), best = 0.
2. For each start index from 0 to n-1: reset running = 0.
3.   For each end index from start to n-1: add arr[end] to running.
4.   If running == 0, update best = max(best, end - start + 1).
5. Return best.
approaches.code:
def max_len_zero_sum(arr: List[int]) -> int:
    # Try every starting index; extend a running sum to every possible end.
    n = len(arr)                      # total number of elements
    best = 0                          # longest zero-sum length found so far
    for start in range(n):            # candidate first index of the subarray
        running = 0                   # sum of arr[start..end], grown incrementally
        for end in range(start, n):   # candidate last index of the subarray
            running += arr[end]       # extend the window's sum by one element
            if running == 0:          # arr[start..end] sums to exactly zero
                best = max(best, end - start + 1)   # keep the longer length
    return best                       # 0 when no zero-sum subarray exists

complexity.time: O(n^2) — every (start, end) window is visited once
complexity.space: O(1) — two scalars beyond the input

approaches.name: Optimal
approaches.intuition: Think of the running prefix sum as an altitude line over the array. If the altitude is the SAME at two moments, whatever happened in between climbed and fell in perfect balance — that stretch sums to 0. So: walk once, maintaining prefix = sum of everything so far, and a dictionary mapping each prefix value to the FIRST index where it occurred. When the current prefix has been seen before at index k, the window (k+1 .. i) sums to zero and has length i - k; keep the maximum. Two crucial details: store only the first occurrence (later repeats measure LONGER windows against the earliest one), and seed the map with {0: -1} so windows starting at index 0 — where the 'previous altitude' is the empty prefix — are counted too. One pass, O(n) time, O(n) map.
approaches.algorithm:
1. Initialize first_seen = {0: -1} (the empty prefix), prefix = 0, best = 0.
2. For each index i with value num: add num to prefix.
3. If prefix already exists in first_seen at index k, a zero-sum window (k+1 .. i) exists: best = max(best, i - k).
4. Otherwise store first_seen[prefix] = i — only the FIRST occurrence, never overwritten.
5. After the single pass, return best.
approaches.code:
def max_len_zero_sum(arr: List[int]) -> int:
    # Equal prefix sums at two positions => the slice between them sums to 0.
    first_seen = {0: -1}          # prefix sum -> EARLIEST index; sum 0 exists "before" index 0
    prefix = 0                    # running sum of arr[0..i]
    best = 0                      # longest zero-sum subarray length so far
    for i, num in enumerate(arr): # single pass over the array
        prefix += num             # extend the running prefix sum by arr[i]
        if prefix in first_seen:  # same sum seen before at index first_seen[prefix]
            best = max(best, i - first_seen[prefix])  # that whole slice sums to 0
        else:
            first_seen[prefix] = i    # record the EARLIEST index for this sum
    return best                   # 0 when no zero-sum subarray exists

complexity.time: O(n) — one pass with O(1) average dict operations
complexity.space: O(n) — the map can hold up to n+1 distinct prefix values

Largest Subarray with 0 Sum.tests:
assert max_len_zero_sum([15, -2, 2, -8, 1, 7, 10, 23]) == 5
assert max_len_zero_sum([1, 2, 3]) == 0          # edge: no zero-sum subarray exists
assert max_len_zero_sum([0, 0, 0]) == 3          # all zeros -> whole array
assert max_len_zero_sum([1, -1]) == 2            # window starting at index 0 needs the {0:-1} seed
assert max_len_zero_sum([1, 0, -1, 1]) == 3
assert max_len_zero_sum([5, 0, 7]) == 1          # a lone zero is a valid length-1 window

Kth Smallest Element in BST.title: Kth Smallest Element in BST
Kth Smallest Element in BST.problemStatement: You are given the root of a Binary Search Tree (BST) and an integer k. Your job is to return the kth smallest value stored anywhere in the tree, counting from 1 — so k=1 means the minimum value, k=2 the second smallest, and so on. Remember what makes a BST special: for every node, everything in its left subtree is strictly smaller and everything in its right subtree is strictly larger. That ordering is the whole key to this problem. You are not modifying the tree; you only read it and return a single integer. k is guaranteed to be between 1 and the number of nodes, so a valid answer always exists.

examples.explanation: The tree has root 3, left child 1, right child 4, and 1 has a right child 2. Sorted, the values are [1, 2, 3, 4] — exactly what an inorder traversal produces: first we go fully left (reach 1), then 1's right subtree gives 2, then we come back up to the root 3, and finally the right child 4. The 1st smallest is 1 and the 2nd smallest is 2, so with k = 2 the answer is 2.
Inorder traversal yields [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6]; the 3rd value in that sorted order is 3.

constraints: The number of nodes in the tree is n, where 1 <= n <= 10^4
edgeCases: k = 1 on a left-skewed tree — the answer is the deepest left node, so your traversal must go all the way down before visiting anything.
k = n (asking for the largest value) — an early-stop solution still ends up visiting every node, so know your worst case.
A single-node tree with k = 1 — the loop/recursion must handle a root with no children without special-casing.
A right-skewed tree (like a sorted linked list) — recursion depth or stack size becomes O(n), not O(log n), which matters for very deep trees.
followUps: If the BST is modified often (insert/delete) and you must query kth-smallest frequently, how would you optimize? (Augment each node with the size of its subtree, making each query O(H).)
How would you find the kth LARGEST element instead? (Run a reverse inorder — right, node, left — and stop at the kth pop.)
Could you solve it in O(1) extra space? (Morris inorder traversal threads the tree temporarily instead of using a stack.)
prerequisites: BST invariant: left subtree values < node value < right subtree values, for EVERY node.
Inorder traversal (left, node, right) of a BST visits values in ascending sorted order — this is the single most-used BST fact in interviews.
How to convert a recursive traversal into an iterative one with an explicit stack (push while going left, pop to visit, then step right).
Python lists work as stacks: append() pushes and pop() pops from the end, both O(1).

approaches.name: Brute Force
approaches.intuition: Forget that the tree is a BST for a moment: any tree lets you collect every value with a traversal. If we gather all n values into a plain Python list and sort that list, the kth smallest is just the element at index k-1. This works on ANY binary tree, which is exactly why it wastes work here: sorting costs O(n log n) even though a BST already stores its values in a recoverable sorted order. It is still worth writing first because it separates the two concerns — 'get the values' and 'find the kth one' — and gives you a correct baseline.
approaches.algorithm:
1. Create an empty list vals.
2. Run any traversal (preorder here): for each non-None node, append node.val, then recurse into left and right children.
3. After the traversal, vals holds all n values in arbitrary order — sort it ascending.
4. Return vals[k - 1], because the kth smallest (1-indexed) lives at 0-indexed position k-1.
approaches.code:
def kth_smallest(root, k):
    # Naive idea: dump EVERY value into a list with any traversal
    # (preorder here), sort it, and read off the (k-1)th element.
    vals = []                          # will hold all n node values

    def collect(node):
        if node is None:               # fell off the tree: nothing here
            return
        vals.append(node.val)          # record the current node's value
        collect(node.left)             # harvest the whole left subtree
        collect(node.right)            # harvest the whole right subtree

    collect(root)                      # O(n): touch every node once
    vals.sort()                        # O(n log n): ignores that a BST is already ordered!
    return vals[k - 1]                 # kth smallest sits at index k-1 (k is 1-indexed)

complexity.time: O(n log n) — O(n) to collect every node plus O(n log n) to sort the list
complexity.space: O(n) — the list of all values, plus O(H) recursion stack for the traversal

approaches.name: Better (Inorder Traversal)
approaches.intuition: The sort in the brute force is pure waste: a BST already IS a sorted container if you read it in the right order. An inorder traversal (visit left subtree, then the node, then the right subtree) hits values in strictly ascending order, because everything smaller than a node sits in its left subtree and everything larger sits in its right. So one O(n) walk produces a sorted list directly — no comparison sort needed — and the answer is order[k-1]. The remaining waste: we still visit all n nodes and store all n values even when k is tiny.
approaches.algorithm:
1. Create an empty list order.
2. Define inorder(node): if node is None return; recurse into node.left; append node.val; recurse into node.right.
3. Call inorder(root) — order is now the values in ascending order.
4. Return order[k - 1].
approaches.code:
def kth_smallest(root, k):
    # KEY FACT: an inorder walk (left, node, right) of a BST visits
    # values in ASCENDING order — the list arrives already sorted.
    order = []                         # values will land here in sorted order, for free

    def inorder(node):
        if node is None:               # empty subtree: nothing to visit
            return
        inorder(node.left)             # 1) all smaller values first
        order.append(node.val)         # 2) then this node's value
        inorder(node.right)            # 3) then all larger values

    inorder(root)                      # one O(n) pass, no sorting needed
    return order[k - 1]                # kth smallest is simply index k-1

complexity.time: O(n) — every node is visited exactly once and appends are O(1)
complexity.space: O(n) — the order list stores all n values (plus O(H) recursion stack)

approaches.name: Optimal
approaches.intuition: We only need the kth value, so why finish the traversal after finding it? Recursion makes stopping early awkward, but an ITERATIVE inorder walk with an explicit stack makes it natural: each pop from the stack hands us the next value in ascending order, so we simply count pops and return the moment the counter hits k. We first slide left from the root pushing every node (those are the smaller values we must visit first), pop to visit, then step into the popped node's right subtree and repeat. Total work is O(H) to reach the minimum plus O(k) pops — for small k on a balanced tree that is far less than visiting all n nodes, and we store at most one root-to-leaf path (O(H)) instead of all n values.
approaches.algorithm:
1. Initialize an empty stack, set node = root, and set count = 0.
2. Loop while the stack is non-empty OR node is not None.
3. Inner loop: while node is not None, push node onto the stack and move node = node.left (descend to the smallest unvisited value).
4. Pop the stack into node — this is the next value in ascending order — and increment count.
5. If count == k, return node.val immediately (early exit — the rest of the tree is never touched).
6. Otherwise set node = node.right and continue the outer loop.
approaches.code:
def kth_smallest(root, k):
    # Iterative inorder with an explicit stack: we can STOP as soon as
    # we have popped k nodes, instead of visiting all n like before.
    stack = []                        # ancestors whose left side is being explored
    node = root                       # current position in the tree
    count = 0                         # how many values we have popped (visited) so far
    while stack or node:              # keep going while anything is unexplored
        while node:                   # slide as far LEFT as possible
            stack.append(node)        # remember this node — visit it later
            node = node.left          # smaller values always live on the left
        node = stack.pop()            # next value in ascending order
        count += 1                    # one more value visited
        if count == k:                # the kth pop IS the kth smallest
            return node.val           # stop early — the rest of the tree is untouched
        node = node.right             # continue the inorder walk in the right subtree
    return -1                         # unreachable when 1 <= k <= n (per constraints)

complexity.time: O(H + k) — walk down one path to the minimum, then k pops; worst case O(n)
complexity.space: O(H) — the stack holds at most one root-to-leaf path

Kth Smallest Element in BST.tests:
# Tree:      3          inorder = [1, 2, 3, 4]
#           / \
#          1   4
#           \
#            2
assert kth_smallest(build_tree([3, 1, 4, None, 2]), 1) == 1   # k=1 -> minimum
assert kth_smallest(build_tree([3, 1, 4, None, 2]), 2) == 2
assert kth_smallest(build_tree([3, 1, 4, None, 2]), 4) == 4   # k=n -> maximum
assert kth_smallest(build_tree([5, 3, 6, 2, 4, None, None, 1]), 3) == 3
assert kth_smallest(build_tree([7]), 1) == 7                  # edge: single node
assert kth_smallest(build_tree([1, None, 2, None, 3]), 2) == 2  # edge: right-skewed tree

Validate BST.title: Validate BST
Validate BST.problemStatement: You are given the root of a binary tree, and you must decide whether it is a valid Binary Search Tree (BST). Return True if it is and False otherwise. The BST rules are strict and apply to EVERY node, not just parent-child pairs: all values in a node's left subtree must be strictly LESS than the node's value, all values in its right subtree must be strictly GREATER, and both subtrees must themselves be valid BSTs. Equal values are NOT allowed anywhere. The classic trap: checking only that each child compares correctly with its direct parent is not enough — a grandchild can satisfy its parent yet violate a grandparent's rule, and your solution must catch that.

examples.explanation: The root is 5, its left child is 1 (fine, 1 < 5), and its right child is 4. Already 4 < 5 is a violation — the right child must be greater than the root. Even worse, 4's left child is 3, which also sits inside the root's RIGHT subtree while being smaller than 5. Any single violation makes the whole tree invalid, so the answer is false.
Left child 1 < root 2 < right child 3, and each subtree is a single valid node, so the tree is a valid BST.
Node 3 sits in the RIGHT subtree of root 5 but 3 < 5 — it violates its grandparent even though 3 < 6 satisfies its direct parent.

constraints: The number of nodes in the tree is in the range [1, 10^4]
edgeCases: A grandchild that satisfies its parent but violates a grandparent (e.g. [5,4,6,null,null,3,7]) — this is exactly what naive parent-child checks miss.
Duplicate values (e.g. [2,2]) — BST validity here requires STRICT inequality, so equal values must return False.
Node values at the 32-bit integer extremes — if you hardcode INT_MIN/INT_MAX as initial bounds instead of ±infinity (or None), a node holding that exact value is wrongly rejected.
A single-node tree — trivially valid; your recursion base cases must not reject it.
A perfectly valid but heavily skewed tree — recursion depth is O(n), so Python's recursion limit can matter for deep chains.
followUps: Can you validate without recursion and without O(n) extra memory? (Morris inorder traversal checks the previous-value invariant in O(1) space.)
How would you find and FIX a BST in which exactly two nodes were swapped? (Recover Binary Search Tree — track the two inversion points during inorder.)
If values could repeat and duplicates were defined to go into the right subtree, how do the bound checks change? (low <= val < high style, adjusting one side to be inclusive.)
How would you count how many subtrees of a given binary tree are themselves valid BSTs? (Post-order, returning min/max/validity triples upward.)
prerequisites: The FULL BST definition: constraints are subtree-wide, not just parent-child — every ancestor imposes a bound on every descendant.
Inorder traversal of a BST yields a strictly increasing sequence, and the converse also holds — a strictly increasing inorder proves the tree is a BST.
Passing information DOWN a recursion via parameters (here: the allowed (low, high) window each node must fit in).
float('-inf') and float('inf') in Python compare smaller/larger than every int — perfect initial bounds that avoid the INT_MIN/INT_MAX trap.

approaches.name: Brute Force
approaches.intuition: Translate the definition literally. For each node the definition demands three things: every value in its left subtree is smaller, every value in its right subtree is larger, and both subtrees are themselves valid BSTs. So for every node we run a full scan of its left subtree checking v < node.val, a full scan of its right subtree checking v > node.val, then recurse. It is obviously correct because it IS the definition — but each node gets re-scanned once per ancestor, which in a skewed tree means O(n^2) total work. The wasted effort: we keep re-verifying the same nodes against one ancestor at a time instead of carrying all ancestor constraints down in a single pass.
approaches.algorithm:
1. Write a helper subtree_ok(node, check) that returns True only if EVERY node in the subtree satisfies the predicate check (recurse left and right).
2. Write valid(node): if node is None, return True.
3. Scan node's whole left subtree with the predicate v < node.val; if any value fails, return False.
4. Scan node's whole right subtree with the predicate v > node.val; if any value fails, return False.
5. Recurse: return valid(node.left) and valid(node.right).
6. The answer is valid(root).

complexity.time: O(n^2) worst case — each node may be re-scanned by every one of its ancestors (skewed tree)
complexity.space: O(H) — recursion stack, up to O(n) when the tree is skewed

approaches.name: Better (Inorder List)
approaches.intuition: Use the signature BST fact instead of re-scanning subtrees: a tree is a valid BST if and only if its inorder traversal (left, node, right) is STRICTLY increasing. Why? Inorder visits the left subtree (all values that must be smaller), then the node, then the right subtree (all values that must be larger) — so any ordering violation anywhere in the tree shows up as some adjacent pair out of order in that sequence. One O(n) traversal builds the list, one O(n) scan checks each adjacent pair with <=, catching duplicates too. The only remaining waste is the O(n) list — we never actually need the whole list, just each value's predecessor.
approaches.algorithm:
1. Create an empty list order.
2. Run inorder(root): recurse left, append node.val, recurse right.
3. Scan i from 1 to len(order)-1: if order[i] <= order[i-1], return False (equal counts as a violation — BSTs here are strict).
4. If no adjacent pair fails, return True.
approaches.code:
def is_valid_bst(root):
    # A tree is a BST exactly when its inorder traversal (left, node, right)
    # produces a STRICTLY increasing sequence — so build the list and check it.
    order = []                          # inorder values collect here

    def inorder(node):
        if node is None:                # empty subtree contributes nothing
            return
        inorder(node.left)              # smaller half first
        order.append(node.val)          # then this node
        inorder(node.right)             # then the larger half

    inorder(root)                       # one O(n) pass over the tree
    for i in range(1, len(order)):
        # any equal-or-decreasing adjacent pair breaks strict ordering
        if order[i] <= order[i - 1]:
            return False                # found a violation => not a BST
    return True                         # strictly increasing everywhere => valid

complexity.time: O(n) — one traversal plus one linear scan of the list
complexity.space: O(n) — the inorder list stores every value (plus O(H) recursion)

approaches.name: Optimal
approaches.intuition: Carry the ancestors' constraints DOWN the tree instead of re-checking them. At any node, all the rules imposed by its ancestors compress into a single open interval (low, high) the value must lie in: start at the root with (-inf, +inf); when we step LEFT from a node its value becomes the new HIGH (everything left must be smaller); when we step RIGHT its value becomes the new LOW. Each node is then checked exactly once against its window — low < val < high — so every grandparent-style violation is caught the moment we reach the offending node. One pass, O(n) time, and only O(H) stack space with no stored list. Using ±infinity (not INT_MIN/INT_MAX) as the initial bounds avoids rejecting extreme values.
approaches.algorithm:
1. Define check(node, low, high) — the subtree rooted at node must keep every value strictly inside the open interval (low, high).
2. Base case: if node is None, return True (nothing to violate).
3. If NOT (low < node.val < high), return False — this node breaks some ancestor's constraint.
4. Recurse left with the window (low, node.val) — going left caps values from above.
5. Recurse right with the window (node.val, high) — going right raises the floor. Return the AND of both results.
6. Kick off with check(root, -infinity, +infinity) and return its result.
approaches.code:
def is_valid_bst(root):
    # Every node must fit in an OPEN interval (low, high) inherited from
    # its ancestors: going LEFT tightens high, going RIGHT tightens low.
    def check(node, low, high):
        if node is None:                    # an empty subtree breaks no rule
            return True                     # so it is trivially valid
        if not (low < node.val < high):     # value escaped its allowed window?
            return False                    # BST property violated right here
        # Left child must stay BELOW node.val; right child must stay ABOVE it.
        return (check(node.left, low, node.val) and
                check(node.right, node.val, high))

    # The root is unrestricted, so it starts with infinite bounds.
    return check(root, float('-inf'), float('inf'))

complexity.time: O(n) — every node is checked exactly once against its inherited window
complexity.space: O(H) — recursion stack only; O(n) worst case for a skewed tree

Validate BST.tests:
assert is_valid_bst(build_tree([2, 1, 3])) is True
assert is_valid_bst(build_tree([5, 1, 4, None, None, 3, 6])) is False   # right child 4 < root 5
# edge: grandparent violation — 3 satisfies parent 6 but sits in root 5's right subtree
assert is_valid_bst(build_tree([5, 4, 6, None, None, 3, 7])) is False
assert is_valid_bst(build_tree([2, 2])) is False   # edge: duplicates are not allowed
assert is_valid_bst(build_tree([1])) is True       # edge: single node is valid
assert is_valid_bst(None) is True                  # edge: empty tree is valid
assert is_valid_bst(build_tree([8, 5, 10, 2, 6, None, 12])) is True

Lowest Common Ancestor in BST.title: Lowest Common Ancestor in BST
Lowest Common Ancestor in BST.problemStatement: You are given the root of a Binary Search Tree plus two values p and q that are guaranteed to exist in the tree. Return the node that is their Lowest Common Ancestor (LCA): the deepest node that has BOTH p and q somewhere in its subtree. Importantly, a node counts as an ancestor of itself — so if p is an ancestor of q, then the node holding p IS the answer. In this implementation p and q are passed as integer values and the function returns the TreeNode object of the LCA (tests read its .val). Because this is a BST — left subtree smaller, right subtree larger at every node — you should be able to beat the generic binary-tree LCA solution.

examples.explanation: Start at the root 6. p = 2 is smaller than 6, so 2 lives in the left subtree; q = 8 is larger than 6, so 8 lives in the right subtree. Since the two targets sit on OPPOSITE sides of 6, no deeper node can contain both of them — 6 is the deepest node covering both, i.e. the LCA. Any node above the split point is a common ancestor, but only the split point itself is the lowest one.
4 is inside 2's own subtree, and a node is its own ancestor — so the node holding 2 is the LCA.
Both 3 and 5 are smaller than 6 (go left to 2), both are larger than 2 (go right to 4), and at 4 they straddle it (3 < 4 < 5) — so 4 is the LCA.

constraints: The number of nodes in the tree is in the range [2, 10^5]
All node values are unique, and both p and q exist in the BST
edgeCases: p is an ancestor of q (e.g. p=2, q=4) — the answer is p's own node, so your loop must return when ONE value equals the current node, not only on a strict straddle.
p and q are the two extreme leaves of the tree — the LCA is the root, and the walk must stop there instead of descending either side.
p and q are direct siblings — their parent is the LCA; a solution comparing only values (not structure) must still land on the parent.
A heavily skewed BST (essentially a linked list) — the descent is O(n), not O(log n), so quoting 'O(log n)' unconditionally is wrong; say O(H).
followUps: How would you solve LCA if the tree were a plain binary tree with no ordering? (Post-order recursion returning found-flags — O(n).)
What if each node had a parent pointer? (Walk both nodes upward measuring depths, or use the two-pointer 'switch heads' trick like intersecting linked lists.)
What if you had millions of (p, q) LCA queries on a static tree? (Preprocess with Euler tour + sparse table / binary lifting for O(1) or O(log n) per query.)
prerequisites: LCA definition, including the subtlety that a node is an ancestor of itself.
BST ordering: comparing a target value with node.val tells you which side of the node the target lives on — no searching required.
Path-based LCA idea (compare root->p and root->q paths) as the generic fallback for any tree.
Iterative tree descent with a single pointer — while node: move left/right — gives O(1) extra space.

approaches.name: Brute Force
approaches.intuition: The definition of an ancestor suggests a direct plan that works on ANY binary tree: compute the exact path of nodes from the root down to p, compute the path from the root down to q, then walk the two paths together from the start. They begin identically (both start at the root) and at some index they diverge; the last node they share is by definition the deepest common ancestor. Finding each path uses a backtracking DFS that pushes nodes as it explores and pops them when a subtree turns out not to contain the target. This ignores the BST ordering completely — each path search may touch all n nodes, and we store both full paths.
approaches.algorithm:
1. Write find_path(node, target, path): append node to path; if node.val == target, report success.
2. Otherwise recurse into left then right; if either finds the target, keep node on the path and report success; else pop node (backtrack) and report failure.
3. Build path_p (root to p) and path_q (root to q) with two separate searches.
4. Walk both paths in lockstep with zip; while the nodes are identical, remember the node as the current LCA candidate.
5. At the first mismatch stop — the last remembered shared node is the LCA; return it.
approaches.code:
def lowest_common_ancestor(root, p, q):
    # Ignore the BST ordering entirely: find the root->target path for each
    # value by searching the WHOLE tree, then compare the two paths.

    def find_path(node, target, path):
        # DFS that records the current root->node trail inside 'path'.
        if node is None:
            return False                    # dead end: target is not down here
        path.append(node)                   # tentatively include this node
        if node.val == target:
            return True                     # found it — path is now complete
        # search both children; if either finds the target, keep this node
        if find_path(node.left, target, path) or find_path(node.right, target, path):
            return True
        path.pop()                          # target not in this subtree: backtrack
        return False

    path_p, path_q = [], []                 # root->p and root->q node trails
    find_path(root, p, path_p)              # O(n) full-tree search for p
    find_path(root, q, path_q)              # O(n) full-tree search for q
    lca = None                              # deepest shared node seen so far
    for a, b in zip(path_p, path_q):        # walk both paths in lockstep
        if a is b:
            lca = a                         # still on the common prefix
        else:
            break                           # paths diverged — stop comparing
    return lca                              # last shared node = the LCA

complexity.time: O(n) — two full-tree DFS path searches plus an O(H) path comparison
complexity.space: O(H) — the two stored root-to-target paths and the recursion stack (O(n) if skewed)

approaches.name: Optimal
approaches.intuition: The BST ordering makes the paths to p and q predictable — so we never need to store them. Standing at any node there are only three possibilities: if BOTH p and q are smaller than node.val, both targets (and hence their LCA) are in the left subtree, so step left; if BOTH are larger, step right; otherwise the two values straddle the node or one of them equals it — and that means this node covers both while neither child can, making it exactly the LCA. The walk visits one node per level with no backtracking: O(H) time, and because it is a simple loop with one pointer, O(1) extra space — beating the recursive form's stack usage.
approaches.algorithm:
1. Set node = root.
2. Loop while node is not None.
3. If p < node.val AND q < node.val, both targets are on the left — set node = node.left.
4. Else if p > node.val AND q > node.val, both are on the right — set node = node.right.
5. Otherwise the targets straddle node (or one equals it) — return node; it is the LCA.
6. If the loop exits (empty tree), return None.

complexity.time: O(H) — one node per level from root to the split point; O(n) worst case if skewed
complexity.space: O(1) — a single pointer, no recursion and no stored paths

Lowest Common Ancestor in BST.tests:
t = build_tree([6, 2, 8, 0, 4, 7, 9, None, None, 3, 5])
assert lowest_common_ancestor(t, 2, 8).val == 6    # targets straddle the root
assert lowest_common_ancestor(t, 2, 4).val == 2    # edge: p is an ancestor of q
assert lowest_common_ancestor(t, 3, 5).val == 4    # siblings -> their parent
assert lowest_common_ancestor(t, 0, 5).val == 2    # deep pair inside left subtree
assert lowest_common_ancestor(t, 7, 9).val == 8
assert lowest_common_ancestor(build_tree([2, 1]), 2, 1).val == 2  # edge: two-node tree

Construct BST from Preorder Traversal.title: Construct BST from Preorder Traversal
Construct BST from Preorder Traversal.problemStatement: You are given a list of distinct integers called preorder, which is the preorder traversal (node first, then left subtree, then right subtree) of some Binary Search Tree. Your task is to rebuild that exact BST and return its root node. A key fact makes this well-defined: a preorder traversal of a BST determines the tree UNIQUELY, because the first element must be the root, the following run of values smaller than the root must form its left subtree, and the remaining values (all larger) must form its right subtree — and this decomposition repeats recursively. You return the root TreeNode; tests compare the tree's level-order serialization against the expected shape.

examples.explanation: The first value 8 is the root. The next values 5, 1, 7 are all smaller than 8, so they form the left subtree; 10 and 12 are larger, forming the right subtree. Within [5,1,7]: 5 is that subtree's root, 1 (smaller) becomes its left child, 7 (larger) its right child. Within [10,12]: 10 is the root and 12 (larger) its right child. Level order of the result is [8,5,10,1,7,null,12] — the null marks that 10 has no left child.
1 is the root; 3 is larger, so it becomes the right child and the left child stays empty.

constraints: All values in preorder are distinct
edgeCases: A strictly increasing input like [1,2,3] — every insert goes right, producing a fully right-skewed tree and exposing the brute force's O(n^2) worst case.
A strictly decreasing input like [5,4,3] — a fully left-skewed tree; in the optimal solution every right-subtree call must return None cleanly.
A single-element input — the function must return a lone node with both children None, with no recursive calls misbehaving.

A value that ends several subtrees at once (like 10 after [8,5,1,7]) — the shared index/bound logic must pop out of MULTIPLE recursion levels without consuming the value early; this is where hand-rolled index management usually breaks.
followUps: Could you build the BST from its POSTorder traversal instead? (Mirror the trick: consume from the END of the list with a lower bound, building right subtree before left.)
Why does preorder alone determine a BST uniquely, while for a general binary tree you need preorder AND inorder? (The BST property replaces the inorder sequence — inorder is just the sorted values.)

If the values arrived one at a time as a stream, could you build the tree online? (Yes — maintain a stack of ancestors; each new value pops smaller stack tops and attaches as a right child of the last popped node, or left child of the stack top: amortized O(1) per value.)
How would you verify a given array COULD be the preorder of some BST without building it? (Same stack scan with a running lower bound — any value below the bound means invalid.)
prerequisites: Preorder traversal order: node first, then the whole left subtree, then the whole right subtree.
BST invariant: at every node, left-subtree values < node value < right-subtree values.

Recursion that CONSUMES a shared cursor: one index moves forward through the input while the call tree mirrors the output tree — a mutable one-element list ([0]) lets nested functions update it in Python.
Passing constraints down the recursion as bounds (here an upper bound), the same pattern used in Validate BST.
float('inf') as a 'no limit yet' sentinel that every real value compares below.

approaches.name: Brute Force
approaches.intuition: There is a beautifully lazy observation: preorder visits the root before anything else, so if we take the values in the given order and insert each one into an initially empty BST using the standard walk-down insert, every node gets created before its descendants — exactly reproducing the original tree. Correctness is free; the cost is not. Each insert walks from the root to a leaf, which is O(h). For a random-ish preorder that is fine, but a sorted input builds a skewed chain, making inserts cost 1, 2, 3, ..., n steps — O(n^2) total. The wasted work: every insert re-walks the same prefix path from the root instead of continuing from where the previous value left off.
approaches.algorithm:
1. Write insert(node, val): if node is None, return a new TreeNode(val).
2. Otherwise recurse: if val < node.val, set node.left = insert(node.left, val); else set node.right = insert(node.right, val); return node.
3. Start with root = None.
4. For each val in preorder (in order!), do root = insert(root, val).
5. Return root — the rebuilt BST.

complexity.time: O(n^2) worst case — n inserts of O(h) each, and h grows to n on sorted input; O(n log n) if balanced
complexity.space: O(H) — recursion stack of the insert walk (O(n) when skewed)

approaches.name: Better (Sort + Preorder/Inorder Build)
approaches.intuition: A different classic fact unlocks a second route: a BST's inorder traversal is its values in sorted order. So sorting the preorder array hands us the inorder sequence for free, and now we have BOTH traversals — the textbook 'construct binary tree from preorder and inorder' recipe applies. Take the next preorder value as the current root, locate it in the inorder range via a precomputed value-to-index map (O(1) per lookup), and everything left of it in the inorder range is the left subtree, everything right is the right subtree. Total O(n) build after an O(n log n) sort — the sort is now the only thing standing between us and linear time.
approaches.algorithm:
1. Compute inorder = sorted(preorder) and build pos, a dict mapping each value to its inorder index.
2. Keep a cursor pre_idx starting at 0 — the next unused preorder element.
3. Define build(lo, hi) for the inorder range [lo, hi]: if lo > hi, return None (empty subtree).
4. Take root_val = preorder[pre_idx], advance the cursor, create the node, and find mid = pos[root_val].
5. Recurse node.left = build(lo, mid-1) FIRST (preorder emits left subtree before right), then node.right = build(mid+1, hi); return node.
6. The answer is build(0, n-1).
approaches.code:
def bst_from_preorder(preorder):
    # A BST's inorder traversal is just its values SORTED. So sort a copy to
    # get inorder, then rebuild with the classic preorder+inorder recipe.
    inorder = sorted(preorder)                   # O(n log n): the BST's inorder sequence
    pos = {v: i for i, v in enumerate(inorder)}  # value -> inorder index, O(1) lookups
    pre_idx = [0]                                # next unused preorder index (mutable box)

    def build(lo, hi):
        # Builds the subtree covering inorder[lo..hi]; empty range => None.
        if lo > hi:
            return None
        root_val = preorder[pre_idx[0]]     # preorder always names the subtree root first
        pre_idx[0] += 1                     # consume that preorder element
        node = TreeNode(root_val)           # create the root of this range
        mid = pos[root_val]                 # where the root splits the inorder range
        node.left = build(lo, mid - 1)      # values left of mid form the left subtree
        node.right = build(mid + 1, hi)     # values right of mid form the right subtree
        return node

    return build(0, len(preorder) - 1)      # cover the entire inorder range

complexity.time: O(n log n) — the sort dominates; the recursive build itself is O(n) with the hashmap
complexity.space: O(n) — the sorted copy and the value-to-index map (plus O(H) recursion)

approaches.name: Optimal
approaches.intuition: We can drop the sort entirely by asking, for each preorder value, one question: does it belong in the subtree I am currently building? Walk the preorder list left to right with a single shared cursor. Each recursive call carries an UPPER BOUND: the subtree being built may only contain values below that bound (left subtrees are bounded by their parent's value; right subtrees inherit the parent's own bound). If the next value fits, it becomes this subtree's root, and we first build its left subtree (bound = val), then its right (bound unchanged). If it does not fit, this subtree is finished — return None WITHOUT consuming the value, letting an ancestor claim it. The cursor moves forward exactly once per value: O(n) total, no sort, no re-walking from the root.
approaches.algorithm:
1. Keep a shared cursor idx = [0] into preorder (a one-element list so the nested function can mutate it).
2. Define build(bound): if the list is exhausted OR preorder[idx[0]] > bound, return None — the next value belongs to some ancestor's subtree, not this one.
3. Otherwise consume val = preorder[idx[0]] (advance the cursor) and create node = TreeNode(val).
4. Build the left subtree with node.left = build(val) — everything smaller than val goes there, and preorder lists it next.
5. Build the right subtree with node.right = build(bound) — values between val and the inherited bound.
6. Return node; kick everything off with build(float('inf')) since the root has no limit.
approaches.code:
def bst_from_preorder(preorder):
    # One pass with an UPPER BOUND: a preorder value becomes a node here
    # only if it fits under the current limit; recursion mirrors the tree.
    idx = [0]                             # shared cursor into preorder (a mutable box)

    def build(bound):
        # Build the subtree whose values must all stay BELOW 'bound'.
        if idx[0] == len(preorder) or preorder[idx[0]] > bound:
            return None                   # next value doesn't belong here: stop
        val = preorder[idx[0]]            # this value is the root of this subtree
        idx[0] += 1                       # consume it — the cursor never rewinds
        node = TreeNode(val)              # materialize the node
        node.left = build(val)            # left subtree: values smaller than val
        node.right = build(bound)         # right subtree: up to the inherited bound
        return node                       # hand the finished subtree to the caller

    return build(float('inf'))            # the root itself has no upper limit

complexity.time: O(n) — the cursor visits each preorder value exactly once and never rewinds
complexity.space: O(H) — recursion stack mirrors the tree height (O(n) when skewed)

Construct BST from Preorder Traversal.tests:
assert tree_to_level_list(bst_from_preorder([8, 5, 1, 7, 10, 12])) == [8, 5, 10, 1, 7, None, 12]
assert tree_to_level_list(bst_from_preorder([1, 3])) == [1, None, 3]
assert tree_to_level_list(bst_from_preorder([4])) == [4]                      # edge: single node
assert tree_to_level_list(bst_from_preorder([5, 4, 3])) == [5, 4, None, 3]    # edge: decreasing -> left-skewed
assert tree_to_level_list(bst_from_preorder([1, 2, 3])) == [1, None, 2, None, 3]  # edge: increasing -> right-skewed

Inorder Successor in BST.title: Inorder Successor in BST
Inorder Successor in BST.problemStatement: You are given the root of a Binary Search Tree and a value x that exists in the tree. Return the inorder successor of x: the node holding the SMALLEST value that is strictly greater than x. Equivalently, if you wrote out the whole tree in sorted (inorder) order, the successor is the value that appears immediately after x. If x is the largest value in the tree, there is no successor — return None. In this implementation x is passed as an integer value and the function returns the successor TreeNode (tests read its .val) or None. The catch that makes this interesting: the successor is NOT always in x's right subtree — when x has no right child, the successor is one of its ancestors, and a clean solution finds it without parent pointers.

examples.explanation: The inorder (sorted) sequence of this tree is [4, 8, 10, 12, 14, 20, 22]. The value right after 8 is 10, so the successor of 8 is the node holding 10. Structurally: 8 HAS a right subtree (rooted at 12), and the successor of a node with a right subtree is the LEFTMOST node of that subtree — from 12 we step left once to reach 10, which has no left child, so 10 is the answer.
14 has no right child, so its successor is the nearest ancestor whose LEFT subtree contains 14 — that is 20 (we stepped left from 20 on the way down).
22 is the maximum value of the tree; nothing comes after it in sorted order, so there is no successor.

constraints: x is guaranteed to be the value of some node in the BST
edgeCases: x is the maximum value of the tree — there is no successor and the function must return None, not crash or return the root.
x has no right child (e.g. x=14 here) — the successor is an ANCESTOR (20), which pure 'go right then leftmost' logic misses entirely.
x is the root with a right subtree — the successor is the leftmost node of that right subtree, not simply root.right.
A single-node tree — the only value has no successor, so the loop must handle root with no children and return None.
x is a deep leaf on the leftmost path — the successor is its direct parent, found because we recorded the parent when stepping left past it.
followUps: How would you find the inorder PREDECESSOR instead? (Mirror the logic: record the node when stepping RIGHT, i.e. when node.val < x.)
What if every node had a parent pointer and you were handed the node itself? (If it has a right subtree, go to its leftmost node; otherwise climb parents until you arrive from a left child.)

If you needed successor queries many times per second, what structure supports successor in guaranteed O(log n)? (A self-balancing BST like an AVL/Red-Black tree — or keep a sorted array and use bisect for static data.)
prerequisites: Inorder traversal of a BST lists values in ascending order — 'successor' means the next value in that order.
The two structural cases for a successor: leftmost node of the right subtree (if it exists), otherwise the nearest ancestor left-turned away from.
BST navigation by comparison: node.val > x means x's successor is this node or in its LEFT subtree; node.val <= x pushes the search right.
The 'best candidate so far' pattern: keep the latest qualifying node while descending, and the last one recorded is automatically the tightest.

approaches.name: Brute Force
approaches.intuition: The definition mentions inorder, so use it literally: run a full inorder traversal collecting the NODES (not just values) into a list — for a BST this list is sorted ascending by value. Then scan from the front and return the first node whose value is strictly greater than x; if the scan falls off the end, x was the maximum and there is no successor. This is bulletproof and even works if the tree were not a BST (after sorting), but it flattens all n nodes and stores them just to pick out one element — O(n) time and O(n) memory where the BST's ordering could have guided us straight down one path.
approaches.algorithm:
1. Create an empty list order.
2. Run inorder(root): recurse left, append the NODE itself, recurse right — order is now sorted by value.
3. Scan order from index 0 upward; return the first node with node.val > x.
4. If no node qualifies, x is the maximum — return None.
approaches.code:
def inorder_successor(root, x):
    # Flatten the whole tree with an inorder walk (which is sorted order),
    # then scan for the first value strictly greater than x.
    order = []                        # nodes in ascending order of value

    def inorder(node):
        if node is None:              # nothing to add from an empty subtree
            return
        inorder(node.left)            # visit all smaller values first
        order.append(node)            # then the node itself (store the NODE)
        inorder(node.right)           # then all larger values

    inorder(root)                     # O(n) time and O(n) extra space
    for node in order:                # scan left to right = ascending values
        if node.val > x:              # first strictly-greater value wins
            return node               # that node is the inorder successor
    return None                       # x is the maximum: nothing comes after it

complexity.time: O(n) — full traversal plus a linear scan of the flattened list
complexity.space: O(n) — the list of all n nodes, plus O(H) recursion stack

approaches.name: Optimal
approaches.intuition: Every node we pass on a root-to-leaf walk tells us something. If node.val > x, this node comes AFTER x in sorted order — it is a valid successor candidate, but maybe not the closest, so record it and step LEFT hoping to find something smaller that is still > x. If node.val <= x, the node and its entire left subtree are <= x, so nothing there can be the successor — step RIGHT without recording anything. When we run off the tree, the LAST candidate recorded is the smallest value greater than x: each new candidate strictly improved (shrank) the previous one, because we only re-record after moving into a region of smaller values. This handles both structural cases (right-subtree successor AND ancestor successor) with one uniform rule, uses no parent pointers, no stored list, and runs in O(H) time with O(1) extra space.
approaches.algorithm:
1. Initialize successor = None and node = root.
2. Loop while node is not None.
3. If node.val > x: this node is a valid candidate — set successor = node, then move node = node.left to look for a smaller (tighter) candidate.
4. Else (node.val <= x): neither this node nor its left subtree can follow x — move node = node.right.
5. When the walk falls off the tree, return successor (None means x was the maximum).
approaches.code:
def inorder_successor(root, x):
    # Walk root->leaf once. Each time we step LEFT (node.val > x) the node
    # we are leaving is a closer candidate; stepping RIGHT never is one.
    successor = None                  # best (smallest > x) candidate so far
    node = root                       # begin the walk at the root
    while node:                       # single descent, no backtracking: O(h)
        if node.val > x:              # this node comes AFTER x in sorted order
            successor = node          # record it — closest candidate yet
            node = node.left          # try to find an even smaller valid answer
        else:                         # node.val <= x can never be the successor
            node = node.right         # so the answer must lie to the right
    return successor                  # still None => x holds the maximum value

complexity.time: O(H) — one root-to-leaf descent; O(n) worst case on a skewed tree
complexity.space: O(1) — two pointers, no recursion, no parent pointers

Inorder Successor in BST.tests:
t = build_tree([20, 8, 22, 4, 12, None, None, None, None, 10, 14])
assert inorder_successor(t, 8).val == 10    # successor = leftmost of right subtree
assert inorder_successor(t, 10).val == 12
assert inorder_successor(t, 14).val == 20   # edge: no right child -> ancestor is successor
assert inorder_successor(t, 20).val == 22   # root's successor
assert inorder_successor(t, 22) is None     # edge: maximum value has no successor
assert inorder_successor(build_tree([5]), 5) is None  # edge: single-node tree

BST Iterator.title: BST Iterator
BST Iterator.problemStatement: You must design a class named BSTIterator that walks over a Binary Search Tree in ascending (sorted) order, handing out one value at a time — like flipping through the tree's values as if they were pages of a sorted book. The class gets the root of the BST in its constructor. After that, two methods are called any number of times: next() must return the NEXT smallest value that has not been returned yet, and hasNext() must return True if at least one value is still waiting to be returned (False once every node has been visited). You are guaranteed next() is only called when a next value actually exists. Nothing is returned or printed by the constructor; the tree itself must not be modified. The interview twist: the follow-up asks for next() to run in O(1) average (amortized) time using only O(h) memory, where h is the height of the tree — so simply dumping the whole tree into a list, while correct, is not the final answer.

examples.input:
root = [7, 3, 15, null, null, 9, 20]
operations: BSTIterator(root), next(), next(), hasNext(), next(), hasNext(), next(), hasNext(), next(), hasNext()
examples.explanation: The tree has root 7, left child 3, and right child 15 which itself has children 9 and 20. Sorted (inorder) order of the values is 3, 7, 9, 15, 20. The constructor returns nothing (null). The 1st next() returns 3 (the global minimum: keep going left from the root). The 2nd next() returns 7 (after 3, the next value up is its ancestor 7). hasNext() is true because 9, 15, 20 remain. next() returns 9 (the smallest value in 7's right subtree), hasNext() true, next() returns 15, hasNext() true, next() returns 20 (the maximum), and finally hasNext() is false — every node has been served exactly once, in sorted order.

examples.input:
root = [42]
operations: BSTIterator(root), hasNext(), next(), hasNext()
examples.explanation: A single-node tree: before the first next() there is one value pending, so hasNext() is true; next() returns 42; afterwards nothing remains, so hasNext() is false.

constraints: The number of nodes in the tree is in the range [1, 10^5].
At most 10^5 calls in total will be made to next() and hasNext().
It is guaranteed that next() is called only when a next smallest value exists.
edgeCases: Left-skewed tree (every node only has a left child): the constructor pushes ALL n nodes because h = n here — the worst case for the O(h) stack, and a good reminder that O(h) is O(n) for skewed trees.
Right-skewed tree: the stack holds only one node at a time, which is exactly why the space bound is O(h) and not O(n) — people often misjudge this case.
Single-node tree: the first next() must empty the stack and hasNext() must immediately flip to False — off-by-one bugs in hasNext show up here.
Many hasNext() calls in a row: hasNext must be a pure query with no side effects; accidentally popping inside it silently skips values.
A next() that pops a node with a deep left path inside its right subtree triggers a burst of pushes — only AMORTIZED analysis (each node pushed/popped once overall) keeps next() O(1) on average.
followUps: Prove the amortized O(1) bound for next(): across n calls, each node is pushed exactly once and popped exactly once — can you explain this to an interviewer in 30 seconds?
Add a prev() operation that steps backwards through the sorted order — what second structure (a 'right spine' stack) do you need, and how do the two stacks interact?
Build an iterator that merges TWO BSTs into one sorted stream (the core of 'merge two BSTs' problems) using two of these iterators and always emitting the smaller front.
Can you reach true O(1) extra space with Morris threading, and what are the risks of temporarily rewiring the tree while a caller iterates?
prerequisites: Inorder traversal of a BST (left, node, right) visits values in ascending sorted order — the single fact this whole problem stands on.
Iterative inorder traversal with an explicit stack: push the entire left spine, pop one node, then jump into its right subtree.
Amortized analysis: a burst of pushes in one next() call is paid for by the pops of later calls — each node is pushed and popped exactly once in total.
Python class mechanics: storing state on self in __init__ and sharing it across method calls.
A Python list works as a stack: append() pushes and pop() pops, both O(1).

approaches.name: Brute Force
approaches.intuition: If we need values in sorted order, the most direct idea is: compute the ENTIRE sorted order once, up front. An inorder traversal of a BST visits values in ascending order, so the constructor can run one full inorder walk, store every value in a plain Python list, and keep an index pointer. Then next() is just 'move the index forward and read the list' and hasNext() is 'is the index before the end?'. This is 100% correct and every operation after the constructor is O(1) — the only problem is memory: we store all n values even if the caller only ever asks for the first two. That O(n) footprint is exactly what the follow-up asks us to shrink to O(h).
approaches.algorithm:
1. In the constructor, create an empty list self.vals and an index self.idx = -1 (nothing returned yet).
2. Run a recursive inorder traversal from the root: recurse left, append node.val, recurse right — self.vals ends up sorted ascending.
3. next(): increment self.idx by 1 and return self.vals[self.idx].
4. hasNext(): return True exactly when self.idx + 1 < len(self.vals), i.e. at least one unreturned value remains.

complexity.time: O(n) constructor, O(1) per next()/hasNext() — the full traversal is precomputed once
complexity.space: O(n) — every node's value is stored in the list regardless of how many are requested

approaches.name: Optimal
approaches.intuition: The aha: we do not need the whole sorted list — we only need to PAUSE an inorder traversal between next() calls. In the iterative inorder algorithm, the explicit stack holds exactly the chain of ancestors we still owe a visit to: the 'left spine' from some node down to the current minimum. So the iterator's entire state is that stack. The constructor pushes the path from the root down its left edge (ending at the global minimum). next() pops the top — that node is by construction the next smallest — and then stages its right subtree's left spine, because the values immediately after it live there. hasNext() just checks whether the stack is empty. The stack never holds more than one root-to-leaf path, so space is O(h); and since every node is pushed once and popped once across ALL calls, n next() calls cost O(n) total — amortized O(1) each. We trade 'precompute everything' for 'remember just enough to resume'.
approaches.algorithm:
1. Constructor: create an empty stack, then call _push_left(root) — walk from the root down left children, pushing every node passed; the stack top is now the tree's minimum.
2. _push_left(node): while node is not None, push node and step to node.left.
3. next(): pop the stack top — it is the next smallest unvisited node.
4. Call _push_left(popped.right) so the successors inside its right subtree are staged for future calls.
5. Return the popped node's value.
6. hasNext(): return True iff the stack is non-empty — an empty stack means the traversal is complete.

complexity.time: O(1) amortized per next() — each node is pushed and popped exactly once across all calls
complexity.space: O(h) — the stack only ever holds one root-to-leaf left spine (h = tree height)

BST Iterator.tests:
# Full walk over a bushy BST
it = BSTIterator(build_tree([7, 3, 15, None, None, 9, 20]))
assert it.next() == 3
assert it.next() == 7
assert it.hasNext() == True
assert it.next() == 9
assert it.hasNext() == True
assert it.next() == 15
assert it.next() == 20
assert it.hasNext() == False

# Edge case: single-node tree — hasNext must flip to False after one next()
it2 = BSTIterator(build_tree([42]))
assert it2.hasNext() == True
assert it2.next() == 42
assert it2.hasNext() == False

# Edge case: right-skewed tree (stack stays tiny in the optimal version)
it3 = BSTIterator(build_tree([1, None, 2, None, 3]))
assert [it3.next() for _ in range(3)] == [1, 2, 3]
assert it3.hasNext() == False

# hasNext is a pure query: calling it repeatedly must not advance the iterator
it4 = BSTIterator(build_tree([2, 1, 3]))
assert it4.hasNext() and it4.hasNext() and it4.hasNext()
assert it4.next() == 1

Two Sum in BST.title: Two Sum in BST
Two Sum in BST.problemStatement: You are given the root of a Binary Search Tree and an integer k. Decide whether there exist TWO DIFFERENT nodes in the tree whose values add up exactly to k, and return True or False. This is the classic Two Sum question, except the numbers are not handed to you in an array — they are scattered across a BST, and you should exploit the BST ordering rather than ignore it. Important details: the two nodes must be distinct (a node cannot pair with itself, so a single-node tree with value v and k = 2v is False), the tree is a valid BST so all values are distinct, and you return a boolean only — not the pair itself. Nothing about the tree may be modified. The natural progression an interviewer expects: check all pairs (quadratic), then a hash-set single pass, then the elegant version that turns the BST into a sorted sequence and runs the two-pointer scan.

examples.explanation: The tree has root 5; left subtree 3 with children 2 and 4; right subtree 6 with right child 7. Its inorder traversal reads the values in sorted order: [2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7]. We need two different nodes summing to 9. Start two pointers at the extremes: 2 + 7 = 9 — an immediate hit, so the answer is true. (Other valid pairs exist too, e.g. 3 + 6 and 4 + 5; any one of them is enough.)
The two largest values are 6 and 7, so the maximum possible pair sum is 13. No pair can reach 28, and the two-pointer scan ends with the pointers meeting — answer false.
There is only one node. Even though 1 + 1 = 2, the two nodes must be DIFFERENT, so the answer is false — a classic trap.

constraints: The number of nodes in the tree is in the range [1, 10^4].
root is guaranteed to be a valid binary search tree.
edgeCases: Single-node tree with k = 2 * root.val: tempting to say True, but the two nodes must be distinct — the j > i (or lo < hi) condition is what silently protects you.
k smaller than min+second_min or larger than max+second_max: no pair can ever match; the two-pointer loop must terminate cleanly with False instead of running off the array.
Negative node values and negative k: the sorted-inorder + two-pointer logic is unaffected, but any 'values are positive' pruning shortcut breaks.
The matching pair being the global minimum and maximum (like 2 and 7 for k=9): it is found at the very first two-pointer step — off-by-one bugs between lo < hi and lo <= hi surface here.
A completely skewed BST (effectively a sorted linked list): recursion depth reaches n, so in Python you must be aware of the recursion limit even though the algorithm is unchanged.
followUps: Can you cut the extra space from O(n) to O(h) by running the two-pointer scan with two lazy BST iterators — one yielding next-smallest, the other next-largest?
What if the tree were a plain binary tree rather than a BST? Inorder is no longer sorted, so which approach survives unchanged? (The hash-set DFS.)
What if the two nodes may come from two DIFFERENT BSTs (LeetCode 1214, Two Sum BSTs) — how do you combine one tree's set with the other tree's traversal?
How would you return the actual pair of values, or count ALL pairs summing to k, instead of returning a boolean?
prerequisites: The defining BST fact: an inorder traversal (left, node, right) yields the values in sorted ascending order.
The two-pointer pair-sum technique on a sorted array: sum too small -> move the left pointer right; too big -> move the right pointer left.
Hash-set membership in Python (x in seen) is O(1) on average — the engine behind the one-pass approach.
Writing recursive tree DFS with a None base case, and mutating an outer list/set from a nested function.

approaches.name: Brute Force
approaches.intuition: Forget the BST structure entirely for a moment: this is just 'do any two numbers in a bag sum to k?'. So collect every node's value into a list with any traversal, then test every unordered pair (i, j) with j > i. The j > i detail is not cosmetic — it guarantees the two values come from two DIFFERENT nodes, which is exactly the rule of the problem. With up to 10^4 nodes this is about 5*10^7 pair checks in the worst case: it passes small inputs but wastes the one gift the problem gave us — the values are stored in a structure that can hand them to us already sorted. Both faster approaches are about cashing in that gift.
approaches.algorithm:
1. Create an empty list vals and run any traversal (preorder here), appending every node's value.
2. Let n = len(vals).
3. For every index i from 0 to n-1, and every j from i+1 to n-1 (j > i ensures two distinct nodes):
4. If vals[i] + vals[j] == k, return True immediately.
5. If the double loop finishes with no hit, return False.

complexity.time: O(n^2) — every pair of nodes may be tested
complexity.space: O(n) — all values are copied into a list (plus O(h) recursion)

approaches.name: Better (Hash Set)
approaches.intuition: The classic Two Sum upgrade: while walking the tree once, keep a set of every value seen so far. Standing on a node with value v, the partner it needs is exactly k - v; if that partner was already seen, some earlier, different node completes the pair — return True on the spot. Otherwise add v to the set and keep exploring both children. Because we check the set BEFORE inserting the current value, a node can never pair with itself, handling the distinct-nodes rule for free. One pass, O(1) average lookups, done. The only blemish: the set can grow to all n values, and this approach never uses the BST ordering at all — it would work on any binary tree, which hints an even more structure-aware solution exists.
approaches.algorithm:
1. Create an empty set seen.
2. DFS from the root; at a None node return False.
3. At node with value v: if k - v is already in seen, return True (an earlier distinct node completes the pair).
4. Otherwise add v to seen.
5. Recurse into the left and right children; return True if either side finds a pair.
6. The value returned by the root call is the answer.

complexity.time: O(n) — each node is visited once with O(1) average set operations
complexity.space: O(n) — the set may hold every value, plus O(h) recursion stack

approaches.name: Optimal
approaches.intuition: Now use the BST for what it is: a machine that produces its values in sorted order. One inorder traversal fills an array arr that is sorted ascending — and pair-sum on a SORTED array is the textbook two-pointer scan from 'Two Sum II'. Put lo at the smallest value and hi at the largest. If arr[lo] + arr[hi] equals k, done. If the sum is too small, the ONLY way to grow it is moving lo right (hi already sits on the largest available value); if too big, the only fix is moving hi left. Each step permanently discards one candidate, so the scan is a single O(n) sweep with zero hashing. The loop condition lo < hi enforces the distinct-nodes rule. Time and space are both O(n) like the hash set, but this version is the gateway to the true space saver: replace the array with two lazy BST iterators (forward and backward) and the same scan runs in O(h) memory — the follow-up interviewers fish for.
approaches.algorithm:
1. Run a recursive inorder traversal, appending each visited value to arr; arr ends up sorted ascending.
2. Initialize two pointers: lo = 0 and hi = len(arr) - 1.
3. While lo < hi (two different nodes are required), compute s = arr[lo] + arr[hi].
4. If s == k, return True.
5. If s < k, increment lo (only a larger left value can raise the sum); otherwise decrement hi (only a smaller right value can lower it).
6. If the pointers meet without a match, return False.

complexity.time: O(n) — one inorder pass plus one linear two-pointer sweep
complexity.space: O(n) — the sorted array of all values (O(h) is possible with two BST iterators)

Two Sum in BST.tests:
t = build_tree([5, 3, 6, 2, 4, None, 7])
assert findTarget(t, 9) == True       # 2 + 7 = 9
assert findTarget(t, 28) == False     # largest possible pair is 6 + 7 = 13
assert findTarget(t, 12) == True      # 5 + 7 = 12
assert findTarget(t, 5) == True       # 2 + 3 = 5 (both in the left subtree)

# Edge case: a single node can NOT pair with itself
assert findTarget(build_tree([1]), 2) == False

# Small trees and negative-friendly checks
assert findTarget(build_tree([2, 1, 3]), 4) == True    # 1 + 3
assert findTarget(build_tree([2, 1, 3]), 6) == False   # no pair reaches 6
assert findTarget(build_tree([2, 1, 3]), 3) == True    # 1 + 2

Recover BST.title: Recover BST
Recover BST.problemStatement: You are given the root of what USED to be a valid Binary Search Tree, but the values of exactly two of its nodes were accidentally swapped with each other. Your job is to repair the tree IN-PLACE: find those two nodes and swap their values back so the tree becomes a valid BST again. You must not rebuild the tree or change its shape — every parent/child link stays exactly where it is; only two node values move. The function returns nothing; the caller inspects the same tree afterwards. The key observation you will build on: an inorder traversal of a valid BST is a strictly increasing sequence, so the corruption shows up as one or two places where the sequence suddenly DROPS. A trivial fix using O(n) extra memory (collect, sort, rewrite) is easy; the interview goal is a single traversal with only O(h) auxiliary space — and the famous follow-up asks whether O(1) space is possible (it is, via Morris traversal).

examples.explanation: The tree is: root 1, whose left child is 3, and 3 has a right child 2. Inorder traversal reads [3, 2, 1] — it drops twice (3>2 and 2>1), which reveals the swapped pair. The first drop marks 3 (a large value appearing too early) as the first culprit; the last drop marks 1 (a small value appearing too late) as the second. Swapping the VALUES 1 and 3 — without touching any pointer — gives root 3 with left child 1 and grandchild 2: inorder [1, 2, 3], a valid BST.
Inorder of the broken tree is [1, 3, 2, 4] — a single drop at 3>2 because the swapped values 3 and 2 are inorder NEIGHBOURS. Swapping them back yields inorder [1, 2, 3, 4].

constraints: The number of nodes in the tree is in the range [2, 1000].
All values are distinct (the tree was a valid BST before exactly two values were exchanged).
edgeCases: Swapped nodes are ADJACENT in inorder (e.g. inorder [1,3,2,4]): only ONE drop appears, so second must be assigned at the first drop too — code that waits for a second drop crashes or fixes nothing.
Swapped nodes are far apart (e.g. inorder [10,2,3,4,1]): TWO drops appear; first must keep the earlier offender while second must be OVERWRITTEN by the later one.
The root itself is one of the swapped nodes: solutions that special-case the root break; swapping values (not nodes) handles it uniformly.
The minimum tree of just 2 nodes ([1,2] with 2 as the left child): prev starts as None, so the guard 'prev and prev.val > node.val' must not blow up on the very first visit.
