            new.random = target        # same position => the matching clone
        old = old.next                 # move to the next original node
        new = new.next                 # ...and to its clone in lockstep
    return new_head                    # head of the finished deep copy

complexity.time: O(n^2) — resolving each of the n random pointers rescans up to n nodes from the head
complexity.space: O(1) auxiliary — only a handful of pointers beyond the n-node copy we are required to build

approaches.name: Better (Hashing)
approaches.intuition: The brute force wastes time re-answering the same question over and over: 'given this original node, where is its clone?' Every answer is recomputed by a linear scan. A dictionary answers that question once and forever: in a first pass, create a clone for every original and record the pair in old_to_new (the original node object itself is the key — Python hashes objects by identity, so duplicate values cause no confusion). In a second pass, every pointer of the clone is a pure translation: clone.next = map[original.next], clone.random = map[original.random], with dict.get gracefully turning None into None. Two clean O(n) passes. The only cost is O(n) extra memory for the map — which the optimal approach will eliminate.
approaches.algorithm:
1. If head is None, return None.
2. Pass 1: traverse the original list; for each node curr create Node(curr.val) and store old_to_new[curr] = clone.
3. Pass 2: traverse again; for each curr fetch its clone and set clone.next = old_to_new.get(curr.next) and clone.random = old_to_new.get(curr.random).
4. dict.get returns None for a missing key, so a None next (tail) or a None random translates to None automatically — no special cases.
5. Return old_to_new[head], the clone of the original head.
approaches.code:
def copyRandomList(head: Optional[Node]) -> Optional[Node]:
    # An empty list clones to an empty list — nothing to build
    if not head:
        return None

    old_to_new = {}                    # maps each original node -> its clone

    # ---- Pass 1: create a clone object for EVERY original node ----
    curr = head
    while curr:
        old_to_new[curr] = Node(curr.val)  # clone stores only the value for now
        curr = curr.next               # node objects are dict keys (hashed by identity)

    # ---- Pass 2: wire next and random by translating through the map ----
    curr = head
    while curr:
        clone = old_to_new[curr]       # the clone of the current node
        clone.next = old_to_new.get(curr.next)      # .get(None) -> None handles the tail
        clone.random = old_to_new.get(curr.random)  # a None random maps to None too
        curr = curr.next               # advance in the original list
    return old_to_new[head]            # the clone of the original head

complexity.time: O(n) — two linear passes with O(1) average dict operations per node
complexity.space: O(n) — the old->new dictionary holds one entry per node

approaches.name: Optimal
approaches.intuition: The hash map exists for exactly one reason: to answer 'where is the clone of node X?' in O(1). The killer insight is that the LIST ITSELF can store that answer, for free, if we place each clone in a known position relative to its original: splice X' immediately AFTER X. The list 1 -> 2 -> 3 becomes 1 -> 1' -> 2 -> 2' -> 3 -> 3', and now clone-of(X) is literally X.next — no map needed. That makes the random wiring a one-liner: for each original curr, curr.next.random = curr.random.next, because curr.next is curr's clone and curr.random.next is the clone of curr's random target. Finally we unweave: restore every original's next to skip its clone, and chain the clones together as the answer. Three O(n) passes, O(1) auxiliary space, and the original list ends up exactly as it started.
approaches.algorithm:
1. If head is None, return None.
2. Phase 1 (weave): for every original node curr, create clone = Node(curr.val), set clone.next = curr.next and curr.next = clone; advance with curr = clone.next so you never re-clone a clone.
3. Phase 2 (randoms): walk the originals in steps of two (curr = curr.next.next). Whenever curr.random is not None, set curr.next.random = curr.random.next — the clone of the random target sits right after the target.
4. Phase 3 (unweave): save new_head = head.next; for each original curr, let clone = curr.next, restore curr.next = clone.next, and point clone.next at clone.next.next (the next clone) or None at the tail.
5. Return new_head — a fully detached deep copy; the original chain is restored to 1 -> 2 -> 3 form.
approaches.code:
def copyRandomList(head: Optional[Node]) -> Optional[Node]:
    # An empty list clones to an empty list — nothing to build
    if not head:
        return None

    # ---- Phase 1: weave a clone right AFTER every original node ----
    # 1 -> 2 -> 3   becomes   1 -> 1' -> 2 -> 2' -> 3 -> 3'
    curr = head
    while curr:
        clone = Node(curr.val)    # fresh copy carrying the same value
        clone.next = curr.next    # clone points at the rest of the list
        curr.next = clone         # original now points at its own clone
        curr = clone.next         # jump OVER the clone to the next original

    # ---- Phase 2: wire the random pointers via the interleaving ----
    curr = head
    while curr:
        if curr.random:
            # curr.random.next is the CLONE of curr.random, because
            # Phase 1 placed every clone right after its original
            curr.next.random = curr.random.next
        curr = curr.next.next     # skip our own clone, land on next original

    # ---- Phase 3: unweave — restore the original, extract the clone ----
    new_head = head.next          # the first clone heads the answer list
    curr = head
    while curr:
        clone = curr.next         # the clone woven right after curr
        curr.next = clone.next    # original skips its clone (chain restored)
        clone.next = clone.next.next if clone.next else None  # clone links to the next clone
        curr = curr.next          # step to the next original node
    return new_head               # fully independent deep copy

complexity.time: O(n) — three linear passes (weave, wire randoms, unweave)
complexity.space: O(1) auxiliary — the interleaved list itself replaces the hash map; only the required output is allocated

Clone Linked List with Random Pointer.tests:
def build_random_list(pairs):
    # Build a random-pointer list from [[val, random_index_or_None], ...]
    nodes = [Node(v) for v, _ in pairs]
    for i, (_, r) in enumerate(pairs):
        if i + 1 < len(nodes):
            nodes[i].next = nodes[i + 1]
        if r is not None:
            nodes[i].random = nodes[r]
    return nodes[0] if nodes else None

def serialize_random_list(head):
    # Convert back to [[val, random_index_or_None], ...]
    order, pos = [], {}
    curr = head
    while curr:
        pos[id(curr)] = len(order)
        order.append(curr)
        curr = curr.next
    return [[n.val, pos[id(n.random)] if n.random is not None else None] for n in order]

# 1) Classic LeetCode example — the structure must be reproduced exactly
pairs = [[7, None], [13, 0], [11, 4], [10, 2], [1, 0]]
head = build_random_list(pairs)
copy = copyRandomList(head)
assert serialize_random_list(copy) == pairs

# 2) DEEP copy: no node of the answer may be a node of the original
orig_ids = set()
c = head
while c:
    orig_ids.add(id(c)); c = c.next
c = copy
while c:
    assert id(c) not in orig_ids; c = c.next

# 3) The original list must be left fully intact (weaving must restore it!)
assert serialize_random_list(head) == pairs

# 4) Edge: empty list clones to None
assert copyRandomList(None) is None

# 5) Edge: single node whose random points to itself
solo = build_random_list([[5, 0]])
solo_copy = copyRandomList(solo)
assert serialize_random_list(solo_copy) == [[5, 0]]
assert solo_copy is not solo and solo_copy.random is solo_copy

# 6) Edge: duplicate values — identity/position, not value, must drive the wiring
dup = build_random_list([[3, 2], [3, 0], [3, None]])
assert serialize_random_list(copyRandomList(dup)) == [[3, 2], [3, 0], [3, None]]

Preorder Traversal.title: Preorder Traversal
Preorder Traversal.problemStatement: You are given the root of a binary tree (it may be empty, i.e. root = None). Return a list containing the values of all its nodes in PREORDER: for every subtree, you record the subtree's root value FIRST, then all values of its left subtree, then all values of its right subtree. In other words the visiting rule at every node is Root -> Left -> Right, applied recursively all the way down. You are not modifying the tree at all — you only read it and build a brand-new Python list of integers in the correct order. For the tree with root 1, left child 2 (which itself has children 4 and 5) and right child 3, the answer is [1, 2, 4, 5, 3]: the root 1 comes first, then the ENTIRE left subtree (2, then its left 4, then its right 5), and only after the left side is completely finished do we print the right child 3.

examples.input: root = [1,2,3,4,5]  (level order: 1 is root, 2 and 3 its children, 4 and 5 under 2)
examples.explanation: Apply Root -> Left -> Right starting at the top. Visit root 1 first — output [1]. Now the entire left subtree of 1 must be printed before node 3 is even considered. That subtree is rooted at 2: visit 2 (output [1, 2]), then 2's left child 4 (output [1, 2, 4]), then 2's right child 5 (output [1, 2, 4, 5]). The left side of the root is now exhausted, so we finally visit the root's right child 3, giving [1, 2, 4, 5, 3]. Notice how 3 — only one edge away from the root — is printed LAST, after the deeper nodes 4 and 5: preorder finishes an entire left subtree before touching the right.

examples.input: root = [1,null,2,3]  (1 has no left child; its right child 2 has a left child 3)
examples.explanation: Visit root 1. Its left subtree is empty, so it contributes nothing. Move to the right child 2 and visit it, then 2's left child 3. Result: [1, 2, 3].
There are no nodes to visit, so the traversal is the empty list — not None.

constraints: The number of nodes in the tree is in the range [0, 100]
edgeCases: Empty tree (root = None) — the function must return [] and not None, and must not touch root.val before the None check.
Single-node tree — both children are None; the answer is just [val], and the loop/recursion must terminate after one visit.
A left-skewed chain 1000+ nodes deep — the recursive version can blow past Python's default recursion limit (~1000), while the iterative stack keeps working.
A right-skewed chain — good for reasoning about space: the explicit stack never holds more than one node at a time, showing space is O(h), not always O(n).
Duplicate values in different nodes — the traversal must be driven purely by tree STRUCTURE; identical values must all appear, once per node, in structural order.
followUps: Write inorder and postorder iteratively — the root is visited LATER in those orders, so a plain pop-and-visit stack no longer works; what extra state do you need?
Morris preorder traversal: can you traverse in O(1) extra space (no stack, no recursion) by temporarily threading right pointers through the tree and then restoring them?
Produce preorder, inorder, AND postorder in a single pass using one stack of (node, state) pairs — a classic Striver follow-up.
Preorder of an N-ary tree — each node has a list of children; in what order must you push them so they pop correctly?
prerequisites: What preorder means: at EVERY node the visiting order is Root -> Left -> Right, applied recursively.
TreeNode anatomy: each node holds val, left, right; None represents an empty subtree (the recursion's base case).
A Python list works as a stack: append() pushes and pop() removes the LAST element, both O(1) — there is no need for a special class.
LIFO consequence: whatever you push LAST pops FIRST — so to process left before right, you must push right first.
Recursion runs on the call stack, and Python caps its depth (default ~1000) — the reason interviewers ask for the iterative version.

approaches.name: Brute Force
approaches.intuition: Honest note first: for tree traversals the 'brute force' is really the natural, textbook variant — recursion — and it is already O(n) time; what we optimize later is HOW the pending work is stored. Preorder's definition is literally recursive: to print a tree, print its root, then print its left subtree the same way, then its right subtree the same way. So the code writes itself: a helper dfs(node) that returns on None (empty subtree), appends node.val FIRST, then calls itself on left, then on right. The machine's call stack silently remembers every node we must come back to. The weakness is exactly that hidden stack: its depth equals the tree height, and Python caps recursion around 1000 frames — a skewed tree of a few thousand nodes crashes with RecursionError.
approaches.algorithm:
1. Create an empty list result that will collect the values.
2. Define a helper dfs(node): if node is None, return immediately — an empty subtree contributes nothing.
3. Otherwise append node.val to result FIRST (that is the 'pre' in preorder).
4. Recurse dfs(node.left) to emit the entire left subtree, then dfs(node.right) for the right subtree.
5. Call dfs(root) once from the top, then return result.
approaches.code:
def preorderTraversal(root: Optional[TreeNode]) -> List[int]:
    result = []                  # collects values in visit order
    # A nested helper lets the recursion share the result list
    def dfs(node):
        # Base case: an empty subtree contributes nothing
        if not node:
            return
        result.append(node.val)  # 1) visit the ROOT first — the "pre" in preorder
        dfs(node.left)           # 2) then recursively print the whole LEFT subtree
        dfs(node.right)          # 3) finally recursively print the RIGHT subtree
    dfs(root)                    # launch the recursion from the top of the tree
    return result                # e.g. [1, 2, 4, 5, 3] for the sample tree

complexity.time: O(n) — every node is visited exactly once
complexity.space: O(h) call-stack frames where h is the tree height — up to O(n) for a skewed tree (plus the O(n) output list)

approaches.name: Optimal
approaches.intuition: The recursion works because the call stack remembers 'nodes I still owe a visit to'. The optimal move is to make that bookkeeping EXPLICIT: keep our own stack of pending nodes, and the recursion disappears. Pop a node, visit it immediately (root first — that is preorder), then push its children. The one subtle point is push ORDER: a stack is LIFO, so to have the LEFT child pop before the right one, we must push the RIGHT child first and the left child last. That single trick reproduces Root -> Left -> Right exactly: the left subtree keeps landing on top of the stack and gets fully processed while the right children patiently wait underneath. Same O(n) time as recursion, but no recursion-limit crashes, and this explicit-stack template is the one interviewers actually probe for — it generalizes to inorder, postorder, and iterative DFS on graphs.
approaches.algorithm:
1. Create an empty result list; if root is None, return it immediately.
2. Initialize stack = [root] — the root is the first pending node.
3. While the stack is not empty: pop the top node and append node.val to result (visit the root of that subtree right away).
4. Push node.right onto the stack if it exists, THEN push node.left if it exists — LIFO order guarantees the left subtree is fully processed before the right.
5. When the stack empties every node has been visited exactly once; return result.

complexity.time: O(n) — each node is pushed and popped exactly once
complexity.space: O(h) stack entries for typical trees, up to O(n) worst case (plus the O(n) output list)

# 1) Sample tree: root 1, left subtree (2 with children 4, 5), right child 3
assert preorderTraversal(build_tree([1, 2, 3, 4, 5])) == [1, 2, 4, 5, 3]

# 2) LeetCode example: right-leaning tree [1, null, 2, 3]

# 3) Edge: empty tree returns an empty list (not None)

# 4) Edge: single-node tree

# 5) Left-leaning chain — root first, then each left descendant in order

# 6) Full 7-node tree: root, entire left subtree, then entire right subtree
